# Camera obscura (`camera_obscura`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by lenses
- Core idea: In a darkened room with one small hole in the shutter, the sunlit scene outside appears on the opposite wall, upside down and reversed, in colour and in motion. It works because light travels in straight lines. A smaller hole gives a sharper but dimmer picture; a convex lens in a larger hole gives a bright, sharp picture at its focal distance. It shows how the eye works, lets one watch a solar eclipse or sunspots safely, and lets a draughtsman trace a view in true perspective.
- Pitfalls:
  - Hole too large (blur) or room not fully dark
  - Forgetting that the image is inverted and promising an upright picture
  - Looking at the sun through the hole instead of at the projected image
- History: china: c. 4th c. BC – Mohist Canon describes the inverted pinhole image; 1088 Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays; greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotelian Problems note crescent sun images under trees during an eclipse; islamic: c. 1011–1021 – Ibn al-Haytham experiments with the dark chamber and writes On the Shape of the Eclipse; europe: 13th c. used for solar eclipses; c. 1500 Leonardo's notes; 1550 Cardano and 1568 Barbaro add a lens and diaphragm; 1558 and 1589 della Porta popularises it
- Read:
  - John H. Hammond, The Camera Obscura: A Chronicle (1981)
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 1: Physics (1962)
